edits.text: - If the left-side stretch is read alone, is it a coherent, self-contained proposition? Most severe when the left span omits the NP head or when the cut separates an obvious head noun or pronoun from its determiners or modifiers (for example splitting a coordinated NP or an "X of Y" nominal), since those cuts fragment reference and can reverse or contradict the isolated left claim; milder when the left span already contains the NP head and the cut only detaches trailing modifiers, nonrestrictive appositives, parentheticals, or additional coordinate items. State the surface distinction the scorer can recognise: "left span contains the head noun/pronoun" (mild) versus "left span lacks the head noun/pronoun" (severe).
edits._was: - If the left-side stretch is read alone, is it a coherent, self-contained proposition? The worst are fragments that lack a diagnosable main predicate or identity of agent when isolated, or cases where a cut splits a noun phrase so the left span omits the NP head or modifiers that determine reference; the mildest are independent clauses, appositives, or clearly parenthetical material, and any left span that already forms a grammatically complete unit — a full clause or a complete NP (head plus required pre/post modifiers) that preserves truth when isolated.

edits.text: When two cuts lie inside the same noun phrase, prefer the cut that leaves the left span a complete NP (includes the NP head) over the cut that fragments the NP.

- Is this marker immediately after a finite copula/auxiliary or other finite main verb and does the following material begin the verb's complement (a noun phrase, adjective phrase, or a that‑clause) that completes its predicate? Bind the verb to its complement: most severe when the following complement is required to determine the verb's core argument or truth conditions (separating them yields a predicate fragment or contradicts the isolated left span); mildest when the continuation is an optional adjunct, parenthetical, or trailing modifier that does not complete the predicate.
